lessons.title: el portal — the big door, and the space behind it
lessons.gloss: the entrance hall — the door made big, and the part of a Spanish building that has no tidy English name

segments.text: Say la puerta. Say el edificio. Between the street and the stairs of a Spanish block there is a space you have no word for. Here it is.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: el portal

segments.text: el portal — the street door of a block of flats, and the hall behind it.
One word covers both the door and the space. Te espero en el portal means downstairs, inside, out of the rain.
puerta plus -al, an ending that makes a bigger or more general thing of the noun it lands on.

utterances: the thing: la puerta. the larger thing: el portal.
the thing: el árbol. the larger thing: la arboleda.
the thing: la rama. the larger thing: el ramal.

segments.text: English has no single word here, which is why translations reach for doorway, entrance, lobby or hallway and none quite fits. When a Spanish word has no clean English partner, learning the situation beats learning a gloss: the portal is where you buzz, where the post boxes are, and where you wait.

segments.instruction: el portal
the door, then the entrance hall
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the door, then the entrance hall]

segments.instruction: I will wait for you in the portal
segments.source: [YOU SAY: I will wait for you in the portal]

segments.text: The street door of a block? (el portal.) Which word is inside it? (puerta.) Does it name the door or the hall? (Both.)

lessons.title: la portera — the person of the portal
lessons.gloss: the concierge — the person who belongs to the portal, and a job with no close English equivalent

segments.text: Say el portal. Say el vecino. There is somebody who is neither a neighbour nor a stranger, and who is in the portal most mornings.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la portera

segments.text: la portera — the concierge, the caretaker. el portero if a man.
She cleans the stairs, takes in parcels, knows who is away, and is the person a notice tells you to leave a key with.
portal and portera share puerta, and the ending -ero / -era makes the person associated with a thing:

utterances: the thing: la puerta. the person: la portera.
the thing: el pan. the person: el panadero.
the thing: el zapato. the person: el zapatero.

segments.text: You met -ería for the place and -dor for the doer. This is the third: -ero for the person whose job is that thing. Three endings, three different questions, and all of them turn nouns you have into words you have not met.
el portero also means the goalkeeper. The one who guards the gate, in both cases.

segments.instruction: la portera
leave the key with the concierge
segments.source: [YOU SAY: leave the key with the concierge]

segments.instruction: the person who works with bread, using the ending
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the person who works with bread, using the ending]

segments.text: The concierge? (la portera.) What does -ero name? (The person whose job it is.) What else is el portero? (The goalkeeper.)

lessons.title: el garaje — spelled to be said
lessons.gloss: the garage — a French word wearing a Spanish spelling, and the floor of the building most notices are about

segments.text: Say el coche. Say la portera. Now name the floor below the portal where the cars live.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: el garaje

segments.text: el garaje — the garage, the underground car park of a building.
Said ga-RA-je, with the j as the throaty jota.
French garage came into Spanish and was respelled. French writes the sound at the end with -ge; Spanish has no such spelling, so it wrote what it heard with the letter it uses for that sound: j.

That habit is worth more than the word. Spanish borrows freely but respells to its own rules, which is why fútbol, champú and chófer look the way they do. A borrowed word you meet in Spanish has usually been made to spell itself the Spanish way, so read it aloud by Spanish rules and the original often appears.

segments.instruction: el garaje

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the car is in the garage]

segments.instruction: why it is not spelled the French way
segments.source: [YOU SAY: why it is not spelled the French way]

segments.text: The garage? (el garaje.) Which language did it come from? (French.) What did Spanish change? (The spelling.)

lessons.title: la norma — what is written on the wall
lessons.gloss: the rule — the heading above every list a building, a library or a pool puts on its wall

segments.text: Say el portal. Say el garaje. Both have a list on the wall. Name what that list is called.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la norma

segments.text: la norma — the rule. las normas — the rules, the regulations.
You meet it in the plural almost always, as a heading: NORMAS DE USO, NORMAS DE PRÉSTAMO.

Latin norma was a carpenter's square — the tool for checking a right angle. A thing that matched it was correct; a thing that did not was off. The word travelled from the tool to the standard itself, and from there into every European language.
That history explains a family you can now read at sight:

utterances: word: la norma. what it holds: the standard.
word: normal. what it holds: matching the standard.
word: enorme. what it holds: out of the square, huge.

segments.text: enorme is the one worth noticing. E- out of, plus norma: outside the square. Something enormous is something that will not fit the measure.

segments.instruction: las normas
the rules of the building
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the rules of the building]

segments.instruction: what enorme has to do with norma
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what *enorme* has to do with *norma*]

segments.text: The rules? (las normas.) What was a Latin norma? (A carpenter's square.) And enorme? (Outside the square.)

lessons.title: junto — together, or beside
lessons.gloss: together, next to — one short word doing two jobs, and the preposition that decides which

segments.text: Say la calle. You can put a thing in a street. Say that two people did something together and see whether you have the word.
juntos — together. junto a — next to, beside.
Same word, two jobs, and the little a is what separates them.

utterances: you say: cenamos juntos. it means: we had dinner together.
you say: junto a la puerta. it means: next to the door.

segments.text: Without a, it describes the people and agrees with them: juntos, juntas. With a, it stops describing anybody and becomes a position — and then it stops agreeing, staying junto whatever follows.
That is a small thing to watch, and it is the sort of small thing a reader trips on: las cajas, juntas is a comment about the boxes; junto a las cajas is where you are standing.

segments.instruction: we went together
next to the portal
which of the two agrees with the people
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two agrees with the people]

segments.text: Together? (juntos.) Next to? (junto a.) Which one changes for gender? (The one without a.)

lessons.title: (portal, portera, garaje, norma, junto) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the five, and of the third ending in three chapters

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say the entrance hall, the concierge and the garage.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three endings, three questions

utterances: ending: -dor. the question it answers: who or what does it?
ending: -ería. the question it answers: where is it kept?
ending: -ero. the question it answers: whose job is it?

segments.text: All three land on puerta or a word like it and hand you a noun you never learned. Do not read a rule into it — many words have no ending at all, and el garaje and la norma in this very chapter came in whole from elsewhere.
What these three chapters have built is a habit: before treating a long word as new, look for a piece you already hold.

You could describe a home. You could not describe a building. La casa, la puerta and el vecino were yours; the hall, the person who cleans it, the car park beneath it and the list of rules on its wall were not.

Those four are where written Spanish actually meets a resident — on a notice, in a message from an administrator, in an instruction about a key. And junto a is the small word that lets you say where any of it is.

lessons.title: (dejar una llave) — read it, then do what it says
lessons.gloss: the payoff — read the notice about the meters and do what it asks

segments.text: Say la portera and el contador. Both appear in the notice you are about to read, and the notice asks you to do something.
Read it once straight through, then answer.
NORMAS DEL PORTAL El jueves vendrán a leer los contadores entre las nueve y las dos. Es necesario que haya alguien en casa. Quien no pueda estar debe dejar una llave a la portera.

segments.text: This is the level's real test, and it is not a conversation. A2 asks you to read a short official notice and act on it correctly. Three chapters ago the words for the notice did not exist for you; the grammar never changed.
Who do you leave the key with? (la portera.) Where do you wait? (en el portal.) What is the heading on the wall? (NORMAS.)
